Gaussian Relational Graph Transformer

Zezhong Ding,   Jin Li,  Xugang Wang,  Xike Xie ††thanks: Corresponding Author   $ˆ†$Equal Contribution Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence and Data Science, University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) Affiliation: School of Biomedical Engineering, USTC Affiliation: Data Darkness Lab, Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research, USTC Affiliation: Chinese Academy of Sciences{zezhongding,lijinstu}@mail.ustc.edu.cn, xgwang@iaii.ac.cn, xkxie@ustc.edu.cn
Abstract

Relational graph learning enables predictive modeling over relational databases by directly capturing dependencies across interconnected tables. While relational graph Transformers extend the receptive field beyond local message passing, a larger receptive field does not necessarily provide more useful information: sampling must preserve relational structure without introducing excessive semantically irrelevant nodes, while attention must account for the temporal relevance of the retained information. We propose GelGT, a Gaussian relational graph transformer that explicitly addresses these challenges. GelGT introduces a structure-semantic collaborative sampling strategy to preserve structural connectivity while filtering irrelevant semantic information, and incorporates a Gaussian graph attention mechanism with a learnable Gaussian bias on the sampled subgraphs to dynamically encode temporal dependencies. We provide theoretical analysis characterizing the structural preservation, semantic refinement, and temporal discrimination of these mechanisms. Experiments on 7 real-world relational datasets covering 21 prediction tasks show that GelGT consistently outperforms existing relational graph learning methods, with improvements of up to 13.8%. Our source code is available at https://github.com/USTC-DataDarknessLab/GelGT.

1 Introduction

Relational databases are widely used to organize interconnected entities across multiple tables in applications such as e-commerce, finance, and healthcare. Predictive modeling over such databases traditionally relies on tabular models (Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Shwartz-Ziv and Armon, 2022; Grinsztajn et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023; Voskou et al., 2024), which typically require manually joining tables and engineering features for individual tasks (Dwivedi et al., 2025; Kanter and Veeramachaneni, 2015; Lam et al., 2021). Recent relational graph learning approaches instead represent rows as nodes and primary–foreign key relations as edges (Robinson et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Fey et al., 2024), enabling models to learn directly from both entity attributes and cross-table dependencies (Cvitkovic, 2020; Fey et al., 2024).

Existing relational graph learning methods (e.g., RDL (Robinson et al., 2024) and RelGNN (Chen et al., 2025)) are primarily built upon message-passing. While effective for local dependencies, message passing becomes increasingly restrictive when useful information lies several hops away due to information decay during propagation (Wu et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022). This limitation is particularly relevant to relational databases, where predictions can require information distributed across multiple tables. More recently, RelGT (Dwivedi et al., 2026) applies Transformer attention over sampled relational subgraphs (Figure 1). This enlarges the receptive field, making it increasingly important to determine which information should be retained and how it should contribute to prediction.

Effective sampling must preserve relational structure while avoiding irrelevant information. Existing relational graph learning methods commonly rely on random sampling (Ranjan et al., 2026; Robinson et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025), which can break connections among sampled entities and lead to structural fragmentation (Meher and Domeniconi, 2025). Increasing the sampled neighborhood can alleviate this problem, but may also introduce nodes that contribute little useful information to the prediction (Menczer et al., 2004). Structural preservation and semantic relevance therefore need to be considered together: structure defines the candidate set, while semantics identifies which distant nodes are worth retaining.

Beyond structural and semantic relevance, the model must determine how the retained information should contribute according to temporal relevance. Useful evidence may concentrate around a specific temporal region and extend over different temporal ranges. An inaccurate temporal focus may direct attention toward irrelevant information, while an overly narrow temporal range may miss useful dependencies and an overly broad one may introduce temporal noise (Guo et al., 2019). Effective relational modeling therefore requires both preserving structurally and semantically relevant information during sampling and explicitly distinguishing its temporal relevance during attention.

To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose the Gaussian Relational Graph Transformer (GelGT in short), as shown in Figure 1. GelGT first introduces a structural-semantic collaborative sampling strategy that preserves relational connectivity while refining distant nodes according to semantic relevance. For the retained information, GelGT further introduces a Gaussian temporal bias into graph attention, where the Gaussian center and range explicitly characterize where and how broadly the model attends over time. We provide theoretical analyses characterizing the structural preservation, semantic refinement, and temporal discrimination of these mechanisms.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We propose Gaussian Relational Graph Transformer (GelGT), a relational graph transformer that jointly addresses structural, semantic, and temporal challenges in relational graph learning through collaborative subgraph sampling and Gaussian graph attention. (2) We theoretically show that structure-semantic collaborative sampling preserves the vast majority (≥99%\geq 99\%) of effective structural information and can effectively mitigate semantic noise in seed node embeddings. We also prove that Gaussian graph attention assigns higher attention scores to temporally relevant nodes and lower attention scores to temporal noise nodes, compared to conventional attention without Gaussian bias (e.g., RelGT). (3) Extensive experiments on 7 datasets and 21 tasks demonstrate that GelGT achieves the state-of-the-art performance on both classification and value regression tasks, with up to a 13.8% improvement in predictive performance.

2 Preliminaries

Relational Database (RDB) (Codd, 1970; Codd, 1979).

A relational database is formally defined as a collection of tables, denoted by ℛ={𝑻1,…,𝑻n}\mathcal{R}=\{\bm{T}_{1},...,\bm{T}_{n}\}, where nn represents the total number of tables. Each row in 𝑻i\bm{T}_{i} corresponds to an entity, which is uniquely identified by a primary key and may contain references to entities in other tables through foreign keys, together with entity-specific attributes and associated timestamp information.

Relational Graph (Fey et al., 2024).

The structure of a relational database inherently forms a graph representation, referred to as a relational graph. A relational graph is formally defined as a heterogeneous temporal graph 𝒢={𝒱,ℰ,ϕ,𝝍,𝝉}\mathcal{G}=\{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\bm{\phi},\bm{\psi},\bm{\tau}\}, where nodes 𝒱\mathcal{V} represent entities from database tables, edges ℰ\mathcal{E} represent primary-foreign key relationships, ϕ\bm{\phi} maps nodes to their respective types based on source tables, 𝝍\bm{\psi} assigns relation types to edges, and 𝝉\bm{\tau} captures the temporal dimension through timestamps.

RDB Task Reformulation.

Based on the relational graph construction, predictive tasks on RDBs can be naturally cast as learning problems on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} denote a target attribute column within a table 𝑻i\bm{T}_{i}. Since each row jj in 𝑻i\bm{T}_{i} corresponds to a unique node vj∈𝒱v_{j}\in\mathcal{V}, predicting a value in the jj-th row of 𝑻i\bm{T}_{i} can be formulated as learning a mapping function ff: 𝒱→𝒴\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{Y} that leverages both node attributes and graph topology. Following previous work (Dwivedi et al., 2026), we focus on two paradigms: (i) node classification, where 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a finite set of discrete categorical labels, and (ii) node regression, where 𝒴⊆ℝ\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R} represents a continuous range of numerical values.

3 Gaussian Relational Graph Transformer (GelGT)

This section introduces the GelGT, as illustrated in Figure 2. GelGT consists of two components: structure-semantic collaborative sampling (Steps ①-③) and Gaussian graph attention model (Steps ④-⑥). The former constructs a query-specific computation subgraph, which enables the latter to learn temporally aware representations. Sections 3.1 and 3.2 describe the two components, respectively.

3.1 Structure-Semantic Collaborative Sampling

The goal of our sampling strategy is to construct a subgraph that preserves structural connectivity while filtering out semantically irrelevant nodes. This yields the final subgraph. The resulting subgraph explicitly defines the valid interaction scope for the subsequent attention model, and is constructed via two stages: (1) structural integrity sampling and (2) semantic refinement.

Stage 1: Structural Integrity Sampling.

The goal of this stage is to preserve the local relational structure around a seed node vv under a fixed sampling budget BsB_{s}. To achieve this, we employ breadth-first search (BFS) to expand from vv. Under the fixed sampling budget BsB_{s}, BFS expands the neighborhood level by level, preferentially retaining information from nodes that are more closely connected to the seed node before reaching farther regions, thereby preserving the local context around vv. During the expansion, we strictly traverse neighbors that satisfy temporal causality11 1 Temporal causality (Prabhakar et al., 2010) requires that the timestamp of any sampled neighbor precedes that of the query node (i.e., τneighbor<τseed\tau_{\text{neighbor}}<\tau_{\text{seed}}), to avoid temporal information leakage., and stop once the sampling budget BsB_{s} is reached. This process yields a sampled node set. Finally, we construct the subgraph induced by the sampled node set. Formally, we define the sampled node set 𝒩sampled​(v)\mathcal{N}_{\textrm{sampled}}(v) and the resulting sampled subgraph 𝒢sub​(v)\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sub}}(v) as:

𝒩sampled​(v)={u1,u2,…,uB},u1=v\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{sampled}}(v)=\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{B}\},\quad u_{1}=v (1)
𝒢sub​(v)=(𝒩sampled​(v),ℰsub),\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sub}}(v)=(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{sampled}}(v),\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sub}}), (2)

where ℰsub={(i,j)∈ℰ∣i,j∈𝒩sampled(v)}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sub}}=\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}\mid i,j\in\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{sampled}}(v)\} and ℰ\mathcal{E} denotes the edge set of the relational graph, and (u1,u2,…)(u_{1},u_{2},\dots) is the BFS visitation order over nodes whose timestamps do not exceed the timestamp of node vv.

Theoretical Analysis.

We theoretically show that the structural integrity sampling effectively preserves the structural information of the relational graph. To quantify this, we use Katz centrality (Katz, 1953) as the topological metric and denote the Katz centrality computed on the full graph and the sampled subgraph as C𝒢​(v)C^{\mathcal{G}}(v) and C𝒢sub​(v)C^{\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sub}}}(v), respectively. We establish the quantitative relationship between the structural loss Δ​C​(v)=|C𝒢​(v)−C𝒢sub​(v)|\Delta C(v)=|C^{\mathcal{G}}(v)-C^{\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sub}}}(v)| arising from structural integrity sampling and the full-graph structural information in Theorem 1.

Theorem 1 (Upper Bound of Relative Structural Loss).

The ratio of the structural loss Δ​C​(v)=|C𝒢​(v)−C𝒢sub​(v)|\Delta C(v)=|C^{\mathcal{G}}(v)-C^{\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sub}}}(v)| arising from structural integrity sampling to the full-graph structural information C𝒢​(v)C^{\mathcal{G}}(v) satisfies:

|Δ​C​(v)|C𝒢​(v)≤0.01\frac{|\Delta C(v)|}{C^{\mathcal{G}}(v)}\leq 0.01 (3)

We provide a detailed proof of Theorem 1 in Appendix A.1. Theorem 1 demonstrates that the structural integrity sampling preserves at least 99% of the effective structural information, ensuring that the sampled subgraph provides a reliable structural basis for subsequent modeling.

Stage 2: Semantic Refinement.

Then, we refine the sampled subgraph 𝒢sub​(v)\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sub}}(v) constructed in Stage 1 to mitigate semantic noise. Specifically, we first encode the raw attributes of all nodes in the subgraph 𝒢sub​(v)\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sub}}(v) to low-dimensional embeddings 𝐡\mathbf{h}. We compute the semantic similarity between the seed node vv and each candidate node uu beyond its one-hop neighborhood via dot product:

s⁡(v,u)=𝐡v⊤​𝐡u,∀u∈𝒩r=𝒩sampled​(v)∖({v}∪𝒩1​(v)),s(v,u)=\mathbf{h}_{v}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{u},\quad\forall u\in\mathcal{N}_{r}=\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{sampled}}(v)\setminus(\{v\}\cup\mathcal{N}_{1}(v)), (4)

where 𝒩1​(v)\mathcal{N}_{1}(v) denotes the set of 1-hop neighbors of vv satisfying the temporal causality constraint1. Among the remaining nodes (𝒩r\mathcal{N}_{r}) in the sampled subgraph, excluding vv and the nodes in 𝒩1​(v)\mathcal{N}_{1}(v), we compute semantic similarity scores and use them to guide node selection. Given the final training budget Bt<BsB_{t}<B_{s}, we first include the nodes in 𝒩1​(v)\mathcal{N}_{1}(v), and then select additional nodes from 𝒩r\mathcal{N}_{r} in descending order of semantic similarity until the budget BtB_{t} is reached. We prioritize one-hop neighbors because the structural contribution of kk-hop neighbors decays with hop distance:

Δ​𝒞k​-hop​(v)=𝒪⁡(βk),\Delta\mathcal{C}_{k\text{-hop}}(v)=\mathcal{O}(\beta^{k}), (5)

where 0<β<10<\beta<1 is the attenuation factor. Hence, one-hop neighbors provide the most important local structural information, motivating their preservation during semantic refinement. Finally, we construct the training subgraph 𝒢final\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{final}} from these BtB_{t} selected training nodes and their edges to vv that satisfy the temporal causality constraint1.

Theoretical Analysis.

Since noise nodes tend to exhibit lower semantic similarity to the seed node, semantic refinement excludes them from the final sampled subgraph 𝒢final\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{final}}. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} denote the aggregated information from neighbors of the seed node, decomposed into semantically relevant information ℐrelevance\mathcal{I}_{\text{relevance}} and noise ℐnoise\mathcal{I}_{\text{noise}}. Semantic refinement therefore increases the relevance-to-noise ratio (by amplifying ℐrelevance\mathcal{I}_{\text{relevance}} and suppressing ℐnoise\mathcal{I}_{\text{noise}}), as formalized in Theorem 2.

Theorem 2 (Enhancement of Semantic Relevance-to-Noise Ratio).

The semantic relevance-to-noise ratio after refinement strictly exceeds that of the pre-refinement stage. Formally,

ℐrelevancebeforeℐnoisebefore<ℐrelevanceafterℐnoiseafter\frac{\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{before}}_{\mathrm{relevance}}}{\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{before}}_{\mathrm{noise}}}<\frac{\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{after}}_{\mathrm{relevance}}}{\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{after}}_{\mathrm{noise}}} (6)

where {ℐrelevancebefore,ℐnoisebefore}\{\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{before}}_{\mathrm{relevance}},\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{before}}_{\mathrm{noise}}\} and {ℐrelevanceafter,ℐnoiseafter}\{\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{after}}_{\mathrm{relevance}},\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{after}}_{\mathrm{noise}}\} denote the semantic relevance and semantic noise before and after the refinement process, respectively.

Theorem 2 demonstrates that our proposed semantic refinement strategy can effectively mitigate semantic noise in seed node embeddings. A detailed proof is in Appendix A.3.

Through structural integrity sampling and semantic refinement, we obtain the final sampled subgraph 𝒢final\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{final}}. The resulting subgraph defines the set of structurally connected and semantically refined nodes used by the subsequent GNN and attention modules.

3.2 Gaussian Temporal Bias-based Attention

The sampling stage determines which nodes should be retained based on structural connectivity and semantic relevance. We next consider how the retained information should contribute to prediction according to its temporal relevance. As shown in Figure 2, GelGT employs a composite architecture that combines a GNN with graph attention. The GNN aggregates local topological information, while the attention module captures dependencies among the retained nodes. To explicitly model their temporal relevance, we introduce an adaptive Gaussian temporal bias into the attention mechanism.

Adaptive Gaussian Temporal Bias.

A straightforward strategy for capturing temporal information, as in RelGT (Dwivedi et al., 2026), is to encode timestamps jointly with other node attributes. However, such integrated representations entangle temporal information with structural and semantic information, making it difficult for the attention mechanism to explicitly distinguish temporally relevant nodes from noise. To address this, we introduce a learnable attention bias that parameterizes a temporal preference distribution via a continuous Gaussian function, allowing the attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant temporal information.

Formally, given the input feature matrix 𝐇∈ℝN×d\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} (derived from the encoders as shown in Appendix E), we define the standard linear projections for the Query (𝐐\mathbf{Q}), Key (𝐊\mathbf{K}), and Value (𝐕\mathbf{V}) matrices as: 𝐐=𝐖Q​𝐇,𝐊=𝐖K​𝐇,𝐕=𝐖V​𝐇\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{W}_{Q}\mathbf{H},\quad\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{H},\quad\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{W}_{V}\mathbf{H}, where 𝐖Q,𝐖K,𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V} are learnable parameter matrices. Different from vanilla self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017), we explicitly inject a temporal bias Biastime\text{Bias}_{\text{time}} into the scaled attention score (𝐐𝐊Td\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{T}}{\sqrt{d}}) before normalization, as shown in Equation 7.

Attention​(Q,K,V)=Softmax​(𝐐𝐊Td+Biastime)​𝐕.\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{Softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{T}}{\sqrt{d}}+\text{Bias}_{\text{time}}\right)\mathbf{V}. (7)

The adaptive temporal bias (Biastime\text{Bias}_{\text{time}}) is formally defined as:

Biastime=Linear​(exp⁡(−(Δ​t−μ)2σ2)).\text{Bias}_{\text{time}}=\text{Linear}\left(\exp\left(-\frac{(\Delta t-\mu)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right)\right). (8)

Δ​t\Delta t denotes the time interval between query and key nodes. Mean μ\mu and standard deviation σ\sigma are learnable parameters. Temporal long-range perception is critical for relational graph learning (Lachi et al., 2025). The learned μ\mu serves to identify the most temporally relevant information (i.e., temporal center) within the long-range temporal receptive field of a training node. Besides, the temporal relevance information decays with increasing distance from the temporal center (Guo et al., 2019). Thus, the learned σ\sigma models the information decay effect, making the temporal bias align with the underlying temporal relevance distribution.

Theoretical Analysis.

In GelGT, the distribution of attention weights is jointly defined by the temporal center μ\mu and scope σ\sigma. This parameterized structure achieves a systematic separation between temporally relevant nodes and temporal noise. First, Lemma 1 proves that the learnable parameter μ\mu converges to the ground-truth relevant timestamp. Based on that, Theorem 3 further proves that our method assigns a higher attention score to temporally relevant nodes than to noise nodes.

Lemma 1 (Convergence of Temporal Center).

Let t∗t^{*} be the ground-truth relevant timestamp. The gradient of the Gaussian temporal bias ℬ⁡(t∗)\mathcal{B}(t^{*}) with respect to the learnable temporal center μ\mu satisfies: ∂ℬ∂μ=ℬ⁡(t∗)⋅t∗−μσ2\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}}{\partial\mu}=\mathcal{B}(t^{*})\cdot\frac{t^{*}-\mu}{\sigma^{2}}. The term (t∗−μ)(t^{*}-\mu) drives μ\mu toward t∗t^{*} during optimization.

Detailed proof of Lemma 1 is in Appendix A.4. Based on the convergence property established in Lemma 1, we further quantify the disparities in attention score assignment between temporally relevant nodes and noise nodes, specifically comparing the mechanisms w/ and w/o Gaussian bias.

Theorem 3 (Attention Score Ratio Enhancement).

Let {αr​e​l​e​v​a​n​tA,αn​o​i​s​eA}\{\alpha^{A}_{relevant},\alpha^{A}_{noise}\} denote the attention scores that the attention mechanism AA assigned to temporally related nodes and noise nodes. Then,

αr​e​l​e​v​a​n​tw/Gαn​o​i​s​ew/G=𝐞⋅αr​e​l​e​v​a​n​tw/o Gαn​o​i​s​ew/o G,\frac{\alpha_{relevant}^{\mathrm{w/\ G}}}{\alpha_{noise}^{\mathrm{w/\ G}}}=\mathrm{\mathbf{e}}\cdot\frac{\alpha_{relevant}^{\text{w/o \ G}}}{\alpha_{noise}^{\text{w/o \ G}}}, (9)

where 𝐞\mathrm{\mathbf{e}} is Euler’s number, “w/ G” and “w/o G” indicate the attention mechanism with and without the Gaussian bias, respectively.

We provide a detailed proof of Theorem 3 in Appendix A.5. Theorem 3 demonstrates that, compared to vanilla self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017), our mechanism increases the ratio of attention weights assigned to temporally relevant versus noisy nodes by a factor of 𝐞\mathrm{\mathbf{e}}. Consequently, our transformer more effectively discriminates between temporally relevant information and temporal noise.

4 Experiments

In this section, we conduct extensive experiments to answer the following research questions:
RQ1: Does GelGT outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of predictive performance? RQ2: How much does each component of GelGT contribute to its performance, and how well can the proposed components be integrated into other baseline frameworks?
RQ3: How do different configurations of GelGT affect its performance?
RQ4: How efficient is GelGT in terms of training and inference time?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets GelGT is evaluated on the recently introduced RDL Benchmark (RelBench) (Robinson et al., 2024). In total, RelBench contains 30 tasks across 7 datasets, covering node classification, node regression, and recommendation. For our evaluation, we focus on 21 tasks on node classification and regression, following the task settings used in RelGT (Dwivedi et al., 2026).
Baselines We compare GelGT with six state-of-the-art baselines for node classification and node regression tasks (Tables 1 and 2). Our baselines include relational graph transformer (RelGT) (Dwivedi et al., 2026), as well as the graph-centric relational database foundation model Griffin (Wang et al., 2025). Consistent with the experimental settings in prior work (Dwivedi et al., 2026), we also evaluate two variants of the Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) (Hu et al., 2020) to further examine the effectiveness of GelGT relative to existing graph transformers. In addition, we compare against LightGBM (Ke et al., 2017), a strong baseline from the tabular learning literature.
Evaluation Metrics Node-level classification aims to predict binary labels for a given node at a specific seed time. We use the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) (Hanley and Mcneil, 1983) as the evaluation metric. Node-level regression involves predicting numerical labels for a node at a given seed time. We use Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as the evaluation metric.

4.2 Performance (RQ1)

We evaluate GelGT on 12 node classification tasks across 7 datasets, as shown in Table 1. The results demonstrate the strong performance of GelGT compared to baselines. Specifically, GelGT improves AUC by up to 6.2% over the baselines. It ranks first in AUC on every evaluated task, indicating its strong ability to effectively distinguish positive nodes from negative ones. Besides, we evaluate GelGT on 9 node regression tasks across 7 datasets, as shown in Table 2. The results demonstrate the best performance of GelGT compared to baselines, achieving up to a 13.8% improvement in MAE. Furthermore, on the very large-scale SALT dataset from RelBench v2 (Gu et al., 2026), GelGT achieves state-of-the-art results across all 8 classification tasks, shown in Table 4. GelGT consistently outperforms a broader set of representative baselines that incorporate recent advances across many evaluated tasks, including the LLM-based approach Rel-LLM (Wu et al., 2025), and transformer-based long-range graph models such as Nodeformer (Wu et al., 2022) and DUALFormer (Zhuo et al., 2025), as shown in Table 4. Additional details on these baselines and the SALT dataset, along with a comparison with RT (Ranjan et al., 2026), are provided in Appendix C.

4.3 Component Study (RQ2)

First, we perform an ablation study by removing key components of GelGT: (1) w/o Structural Integrity Sampling: We use random sampling instead. This does not preserve the topological structure of the relational graph. (2) w/o Semantic Refinement: We retain all sampled nodes, including the irrelevant ones. (3) w/o Adaptive Gaussian Temporal Bias: We remove the adaptive Gaussian temporal bias, reducing the attention mechanism to vanilla self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017). Tables 5 and 6 present the ablation study results for the node classification and node regression tasks, respectively. In Tables 5 and 6, removing structural integrity sampling degrades performance, confirming the necessity of the topological structure preserved by our sampling strategy. Eliminating semantic refinement leads to a clear drop, demonstrating that GelGT effectively removes irrelevant information. Finally, excluding the adaptive Gaussian temporal bias results in an observable performance loss, indicating that simply encoding time as features is insufficient.

Besides, we evaluate the performance of RelGT enhanced with our proposed key components, including structural-semantic collaborative sampling and Gaussian temporal bias, across five different tasks to validate their effectiveness. As shown in Figure 3, this uniform performance gain across diverse tasks demonstrates that our approach effectively addresses the limitations of the original framework. In summary, the results demonstrate that our proposed modules effectively generalize to other baseline frameworks, significantly enhancing their predictive performance. In Appendix F.2, we further demonstrate through experiments that the proposed sampling strategy is model-agnostic and can improve the predictive performance of RelGNN (Chen et al., 2025).

What is more, we conduct more fine-grained ablation studies to validate the rationale behind several of our design choices, including the GNN branch, selection rule, traversal strategy, and temporal bias as follows. (1) GNN Branch. As shown in Table 7, performance consistently drops across all datasets. This validates the necessity of the GNN branch in GelGT. The attention branch, even with hop-distance embeddings and GNN-based positional encodings, operates on a fully connected sampled subgraph and therefore only captures relative positional information, without explicitly modeling the true PK-FK edges. In contrast, the GNN branch performs message passing directly along PK-FK edges, which preserves the original relational structure and better captures the semantic dependencies encoded in these edges. (2) Selection Rule. Top-kk selection by the dot-product score beats both random-kk and bottom-kk drawn from the same candidate pool on all five tasks (Table 8 (a)), confirming that the score ranks nodes by downstream usefulness rather than acting as an arbitrary heuristic. (3) Traversal Strategy. BFS beats DFS on all five tasks, with the largest relative gain of 2.1% on study-outcome (Table 8 (b)). This advantage stems from their different traversal patterns under a fixed sampling budget. DFS preferentially explores a single PK–FK branch, concentrating samples on a few relational paths and leaving other direct PK–FK neighbors uncovered. In contrast, BFS expands PK–FK neighbors level by level, providing broader relational coverage within the same budget. (4) Other Temporal Biases. Our Gaussian bias beats both a scaled linear bias and a learnable temporal embedding on all seven datasets (Table 8 (c)). (5) Temporal Bias under Temporal Shuffling. Under temporal shuffling (i.e., randomly shuffling the timestamps of the dataset to make the evaluation more challenging), w/o temporal bias (i.e., RelGT’s attention) experiences an average decline of 0.0441 (5.64%), while w/ temporal bias (i.e., GelGT) exhibits a smaller drop of 0.0348 (4.36%) (Table 8 (d)). This suggests that incorporating temporal bias into the attention mechanism improves its robustness to temporal perturbations.

4.4 Configuration Analysis (RQ3)

Sampling Size Analysis. We vary the number of sampled nodes (i.e., sampling size) within {100,200,300,400,500}\{100,200,300,400,500\}, as shown in Figure 5. The performance across all tasks reaches its peak at a sampling size of 300. Specifically, when the sampling size is less than 300, the model suffers from an information bottleneck and fails to capture sufficient semantic information. Conversely, when the sampling size exceeds 300, the limited number of truly relevant neighbors forces the similarity-based mechanism to incorporate semantically irrelevant nodes, which obscures the contribution of semantically relevant nodes. Therefore, we set the sampling size to 300, as it ensures sufficient information aggregation while avoiding interference from semantically irrelevant nodes. In the Appendix F.6, we further analyze the sampling budget.

Sampling Hop Analysis. Then, we vary the sampling hops from {2,3,4,5}\{2,3,4,5\}, as summarized in Figure 5. The performance remains consistent across all tasks with minimal fluctuations, indicating that GelGT is insensitive to the sampling hops. In GelGT, long-range information is incorporated through the semantic relevance-based selection of distant nodes in Stage 2, rather than through indiscriminate topological expansion. This stability suggests that increasing the search depth beyond a moderate range provides limited benefit once semantic refinement is applied. Stage 1 exposes candidate nodes through topological expansion, while Stage 2 selectively retains distant nodes according to semantic relevance. Consequently, deeper expansion mainly increases the candidate pool and computational cost, rather than proportionally increasing useful information. Details on the rationale behind the semantic refinement design are provided in Appendix F.1.

4.5 Efficiency Analysis (RQ4)

We evaluate the efficiency of GelGT across five tasks by comparing its training time per epoch and inference time against state-of-the-art relational graph transformer models. As shown in Figure 6, GelGT consistently demonstrates lower time costs for both training and inference across all five evaluated tasks compared to baseline methods. This uniform reduction in computational overhead confirms that GelGT is more efficient for relational graph learning tasks.

This advantage does not come at the cost of attention computation efficiency: at the 300-node context we use, our attention costs only 1.07×\times the epoch time of FlashAttention (Table 10). Furthermore, we evaluate our sampling efficiency in comparison with naive Random Sampling. Empirical results from Table 10 demonstrate that combining Breadth-First Search (BFS) with semantic similarity-based refinement introduces negligible latency, maintaining a computational cost highly comparable to Random Sampling. Appendix D further analyzes sampling latency, attention cost, and memory consumption under increasing context sizes.

5 Conclusion

We present GelGT, a Gaussian Relational Graph Transformer that improves long-range relational modeling by determining both which information to retain and how it should contribute to prediction. GelGT combines structure-semantic collaborative sampling to preserve relevant relational information with a Gaussian temporal bias to model its temporal focus and range. Experiments on 7 real-world relational datasets covering 21 prediction tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing relational graph learning methods.

Appendix A Proofs of Theorems.

A.1 Upper Bound of Relative Structural Loss

Proof. To characterize the multi-hop topological structure of nodes in the graph, we employ Katz centrality (Katz, 1953) as our analytical tool. As a classic walk-based topological metric, Katz centrality systematically captures the structural reach of a node by computing a weighted sum of all walks of varying lengths associated with it. Formally, let AA be the adjacency matrix of the graph, and λ\lambda be the attenuation factor determining the weight decay of paths. Let 𝐂𝒢\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}} denote the vector of Katz centrality for all nodes in the full graph, and let 𝟏\mathbf{1} be the vector of all ones. The matrix-vector form of Katz centrality is given by the Neumann series:

𝐂𝒢=∑k=1∞(λ​A)k​𝟏.\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\lambda A)^{k}\mathbf{1}. (10)

The structural integrity sampling strategy preserves all walks of length k=1k=1 and k=2k=2. The structural loss vector 𝚫​𝑪\bm{\Delta C}, which consists of all walks of length k≥3k\geq 3, can be expressed as:

𝚫​𝑪=∑k=3∞(λ​A)k​𝟏.\bm{\Delta C}=\sum_{k=3}^{\infty}(\lambda A)^{k}\mathbf{1}. (11)

We observe a critical recursive relationship between the error vector and the global centrality vector. By factoring out (λ​A)2(\lambda A)^{2} from the error series:

𝚫​𝑪=(λ​A)2​(∑k=1∞(λ​A)k​𝟏)=(λ​A)2​𝐂𝒢.\bm{\Delta C}=(\lambda A)^{2}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(\lambda A)^{k}\mathbf{1}\right)=(\lambda A)^{2}\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}}. (12)

To quantify the relative magnitude of the loss, we employ the matrix 2-norm (spectral norm). Using the consistency property of matrix norms (‖M​𝐱‖≤‖M‖​‖𝐱‖\|M\mathbf{x}\|\leq\|M\|\|\mathbf{x}\|), we have:

‖𝚫​𝑪‖2=‖(λ​A)2​𝐂𝒢‖2≤‖(λ​A)2‖2​‖𝐂𝒢‖2.\|\bm{\Delta C}\|_{2}=\|(\lambda A)^{2}\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}}\|_{2}\leq\|(\lambda A)^{2}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}}\|_{2}. (13)

Using the property that the spectral norm of a symmetric matrix is its spectral radius, i.e., ‖A‖2=ρ⁡(A)\|A\|_{2}=\rho(A), and considering the definition λ=c/ρ⁡(A)\lambda=c/\rho(A):

‖(λ​A)2‖2≤(λ​‖A‖2)2=(λ​ρ​(A))2=(cρ⁡(A)⋅ρ⁡(A))2=c2.\|(\lambda A)^{2}\|_{2}\leq(\lambda\|A\|_{2})^{2}=(\lambda\rho(A))^{2}=\left(\frac{c}{\rho(A)}\cdot\rho(A)\right)^{2}=c^{2}. (14)

Substituting this bound back into the inequality yields:

‖𝚫​𝑪‖2≤c2​‖𝐂𝒢‖2.\|\bm{\Delta C}\|_{2}\leq c^{2}\|\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}}\|_{2}. (15)

Rearranging the terms, we obtain the strict upper bound for the relative structural loss:

‖𝚫​𝑪‖2‖𝐂𝒢‖2≤c2.\frac{\|\bm{\Delta C}\|_{2}}{\|\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}}\|_{2}}\leq c^{2}. (16)

Following the analysis of the local regime by Benzi and Klymko (Benzi and Klymko, 2013), the scaling factor cc falls within the range of ≤0.1\leq 0.1.

Substituting this value into Theorem 1, the relative structural loss is upper-bounded by:

‖𝚫​𝑪‖2‖𝐂𝒢‖2≤(0.1)2=1%.\frac{\|\bm{\Delta C}\|_{2}}{\|\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{G}}\|_{2}}\leq(0.1)^{2}=1\%. (17)

This confirms that under standard operating conditions, the structural integrity sampling preserves at least 99% of the effective structural information.

A.2 Exponential Decay of Structural Sensitivity

proof. To justify the differentiated pruning strategy in Stage 2, we analyze the sensitivity of the seed node’s structural information to the removal of a specific neighbor at distance kk. We define the structural sensitivity Δ​𝒞​(v,k)\Delta\mathcal{C}(v,k) as the magnitude of change in the Katz centrality of vv when a node uu at distance kk (i.e., dist​(v,u)=k\text{dist}(v,u)=k) is removed from the graph.

Based on the definition of Katz centrality, the contribution of a node uu to vv is the weighted sum of all walks between them:

Contr(u→v)=∑γ:u↝vβ|γ|,\text{Contr}(u\to v)=\sum_{\gamma:u\rightsquigarrow v}\beta^{|\gamma|}, (18)

where γ\gamma represents a walk from uu to vv, β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) is the attenuation factor determining the weight decay of paths and |γ||\gamma| is its length.

When a neighbor uu at distance kk is pruned, all walks passing through uu are eliminated. The dominant term in this summation corresponds to the shortest path (geodesic) of length kk. Higher-order paths (length >k>k) also contribute, but their weights are dampened by higher powers of β\beta. Therefore, the structural loss is dominated by the leading term:

Δ​𝒞k−h​o​p​(v)≈βk⋅Npaths​(k)+𝒪⁡(βk+1),\Delta\mathcal{C}_{k-hop}(v)\approx\beta^{k}\cdot N_{\text{paths}}(k)+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{k+1}), (19)

where Npaths​(k)N_{\text{paths}}(k) denotes the number of shortest paths of length kk between vv and uu (typically small for local neighborhoods).

Now, we compare the sensitivity at k=1k=1 (direct neighbors) and k=2k=2 (two-hop neighbors):

Δ​𝒞1−h​o​p​(v)\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{C}_{1-hop}(v) =β⋅1+𝒪⁡(β2)∼𝒪⁡(β),\displaystyle=\beta\cdot 1+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{2})\sim\mathcal{O}(\beta), (20)
Δ​𝒞2−h​o​p​(v)\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{C}_{2-hop}(v) =β2⋅Npaths​(2)+𝒪⁡(β3)∼𝒪⁡(β2).\displaystyle=\beta^{2}\cdot N_{\text{paths}}(2)+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{3})\sim\mathcal{O}(\beta^{2}). (21)

Note that for k=1k=1, there is exactly one direct edge, so the coefficient is 1.

The ratio of structural sensitivity between pruning a 2-hop neighbor and a 1-hop neighbor is:

Δ​𝒞2−h​o​p​(v)Δ​𝒞1−h​o​p​(v)≈𝒪⁡(β2)𝒪⁡(β)=𝒪⁡(β).\frac{\Delta\mathcal{C}_{2-hop}(v)}{\Delta\mathcal{C}_{1-hop}(v)}\approx\frac{\mathcal{O}(\beta^{2})}{\mathcal{O}(\beta)}=\mathcal{O}(\beta). (22)

Since the attenuation factor β\beta is typically chosen to be small (satisfying β<1/ρ⁡(A)\beta<1/\rho(A)), this ratio indicates that the structural perturbation caused by removing a 2-hop neighbor is an order of magnitude smaller than that of removing a 1-hop neighbor. This theoretical result confirms that 1-hop neighbors form the non-negligible structural skeleton (𝒪⁡(β)\mathcal{O}(\beta) sensitivity), whereas 2-hop neighbors allow for aggressive semantic pruning with bounded structural risk (𝒪⁡(β2)\mathcal{O}(\beta^{2}) sensitivity). ∎

A.3 Enhancement of Semantic Relevance-to-Noise Ratio

As we prove in Appendix A.2, pruning 2-hop neighbors has a much smaller impact on structural information compared to 1-hop neighbors. Therefore, we apply the following semantic refinement exclusively to 2-hop neighbors.

Proof. The features of the sampled neighbors are aggregated to obtain a representation for the seed node, which is then used for downstream tasks. We define a general aggregation formula as follows:

𝐡a​g​g=∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​𝐡u\mathbf{h}_{agg}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\mathbf{h}_{u} (23)

In this formulation, vv represents the seed node, uu is a neighbor of vv, 𝐡u\mathbf{h}_{u} denotes the feature of neighbor uu, w⁡(v,u)w(v,u) is the aggregation weight, and 𝐡agg\mathbf{h}_{\text{agg}} corresponds to the aggregated feature.

We can decompose the feature of neighbor uu, 𝐡u\mathbf{h}_{u}, into a part that is semantically relevant to the seed node and a part that corresponds to irrelevant noise:

𝐡u=μv​u​𝐡v+𝐡unoise\mathbf{h}_{u}=\mu_{vu}\mathbf{h}_{v}+\mathbf{h}_{u}^{\text{noise}} (24)

The first term corresponds to the part of 𝐡u\mathbf{h}_{u} that is semantically relevant to the seed node vv, with μv​u\mu_{vu} representing the degree of relevance. The second term represents the part unrelated to vv, i.e., random noise (e.g., heterophily), assumed to have variance σnoise2\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}.

By substituting 𝐡u\mathbf{h}_{u} into the aggregation formula, we can decompose the aggregated feature into two parts:

𝐡agg=∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​𝐡u=∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​μv​u​𝐡v⏟semantically relevant+∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​𝐡unoise⏟noise\mathbf{h}_{\text{agg}}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\mathbf{h}_{u}=\underbrace{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\mu_{vu}\mathbf{h}_{v}}_{\text{semantically relevant}}+\underbrace{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\mathbf{h}_{u}^{\text{noise}}}_{\text{noise}} (25)

Following the theoretical analysis in PairNorm (Zhao and Akoglu, 2020), which establishes that the information content of node features is strictly proportional to their squared norm, we measure the magnitude of the aggregated information using the L2L_{2}-norm. Therefore, the aggregated semantically relevant information is quantified as:

ℐrelevance=‖(∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​μv​u)​𝐡v‖2=(∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​μu​v)2⋅‖𝐡v‖2\mathcal{I}_{\text{relevance}}=\left\|\left(\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\,\mu_{vu}\right)\mathbf{h}_{v}\right\|^{2}=\left(\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\mu_{uv}\right)^{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{h}_{v}\|^{2} (26)

The variance directly measures the destructive information or uncertainty (Kendall and Gal, 2017) introduced by irrelevant neighbors. Therefore, we compute the semantically noisy information as:

ℐnoise=∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)Var⁡(w⁡(v,u)​𝐡unoise)\mathcal{I}_{\text{noise}}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\mathrm{Var}(w(v,u)\mathbf{h}_{u}^{\text{noise}}) (27)

Using the properties of variance, we can factor out the weight w⁡(v,u)w(v,u) to obtain:

ℐnoise=∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w​(v,u)2​Var​(𝐡unoise)\mathcal{I}_{\text{noise}}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{h}_{u}^{\text{noise}}) (28)

If the variance of each individual noise is σnoise2\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}:

ℐnoise=∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w​(v,u)2​σnoise2=σnoise2​∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w​(v,u)2\mathcal{I}_{\text{noise}}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)^{2}\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}=\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)^{2} (29)

Therefore, the ratio of relevant information to noise information is:

SNR=ℐrelevanceℐn​o​i​s​e=(∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​μu​v)2⋅‖𝐡v‖2σnoise2​∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w​(v,u)2=‖𝐡v‖2σnoise2⏟constant⋅(∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w⁡(v,u)​μu​v)2∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)w​(v,u)2\text{SNR}=\frac{\mathcal{I}_{\text{relevance}}}{\mathcal{I}_{noise}}=\frac{\left(\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\mu_{uv}\right)^{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{h}_{v}\|^{2}}{\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)^{2}}=\underbrace{\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_{v}\|^{2}}{\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}}}_{\text{constant}}\cdot\frac{\left(\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)\mu_{uv}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}w(v,u)^{2}} (30)

To demonstrate the effectiveness of our semantic refinement, we denote the refined 2-hop neighbors by 𝒩r​e​f​i​n​e​(v)\mathcal{N}_{refine}(v) and the remaining subsets is denoted as 𝒩r​e​m​a​i​n​i​n​g​(v)\mathcal{N}_{remaining}(v).

Let AA and BB denote the relevance term and noise term in SNR of our refinement strategy, respectively:

A=∑u∈𝒩r​e​f​i​n​e​(v)w⁡(v,u)​μv​u,B=∑u∈𝒩r​e​f​i​n​e​(v)w​(v,u)2.A=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}_{refine}(v)}w(v,u)\mu_{vu},\quad B=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}_{refine}(v)}w(v,u)^{2}. (31)

Similarly, for the remaining subset 𝒩r​e​m​a​i​n​i​n​g​(v)\mathcal{N}_{remaining}(v), we define the relevance term aa and noise term bb:

a=∑u∈𝒩r​e​m​a​i​n​i​n​g​(v)w⁡(v,u)​μv​u,b=∑u∈𝒩r​e​m​a​i​n​i​n​g​(v)w​(v,u)2a=\sum_{u\in{\mathcal{N}_{remaining}(v)}}w(v,u)\mu_{vu},\quad b=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}_{remaining}(v)}w(v,u)^{2} (32)

Nodes in 𝒩r​e​m​a​i​n​i​n​g​(v)\mathcal{N}_{remaining}(v) have negligible correlation with the seed node, implying μv​u≈0\mu_{vu}\approx 0 and thus a≈0a\approx 0. However, since these nodes objectively exist in the graph, they contribute a strictly positive noise term, i.e., b>0b>0.

Now, we compare the SNR of our refinement strategy (SNRp​o​s​t\text{SNR}_{post}) against the full 2-hop neighborhood strategy (SNRp​r​e\text{SNR}_{pre}):

SNRa​f​t​e​r=ℐrelevancea​f​t​e​rℐnoisea​f​t​e​r=‖𝐡v‖2σnoise2⋅A2B\text{SNR}_{after}=\frac{\mathcal{I}^{after}_{\text{relevance}}}{\mathcal{I}^{after}_{\text{noise}}}=\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_{v}\|^{2}}{\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}}\cdot\frac{A^{2}}{B} (33)
SNRb​e​f​o​r​e=ℐrelevanceb​e​f​o​r​eℐnoiseb​e​f​o​r​e=‖𝐡v‖2σnoise2⋅(A+a)2B+b≈‖𝐡v‖2σnoise2⋅A2B+b.\text{SNR}_{before}=\frac{\mathcal{I}^{before}_{\text{relevance}}}{\mathcal{I}^{before}_{\text{noise}}}=\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_{v}\|^{2}}{\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}}\cdot\frac{(A+a)^{2}}{B+b}\approx\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_{v}\|^{2}}{\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}}\cdot\frac{A^{2}}{B+b}. (34)

Since bb is positive and BB is positive, the denominator of the full 2-hop neighborhood strategy is strictly larger while the numerator remains approximately unchanged. This leads to the inequality:

A2B+b<A2B⟹SNRb​e​f​o​r​e<SNRa​f​t​e​r⟹ℐrelevanceb​e​f​o​r​eℐnoiseb​e​f​o​r​e<ℐrelevancea​f​t​e​rℐnoisea​f​t​e​r.\frac{A^{2}}{B+b}<\frac{A^{2}}{B}\implies\text{SNR}_{before}<\text{SNR}_{after}\implies\frac{\mathcal{I}^{before}_{\text{relevance}}}{\mathcal{I}^{before}_{\text{noise}}}<\frac{\mathcal{I}^{after}_{\text{relevance}}}{\mathcal{I}^{after}_{\text{noise}}}. (35)

This inequality mathematically guarantees that pruning low-similarity neighbors effectively removes the noise denominator bb without sacrificing the relevance term numerator AA, thereby strictly maximizing the ratio of relevant information to noise information of the aggregated representation. Consequently, this result rigorously confirms that our semantic refinement strategy functions as an effective denoising filter, eliminating irrelevant nodes to enhance the quality of node representation. ∎

A.4 Convergence of Temporal Center

In this subsection, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that the proposed attention mechanism is able to focus more effectively on temporally relevant nodes compared to existing attention mechanisms.

For the model to attend to relevant historical information, the learnable temporal center μ\mu must converge to the ground-truth relevant timestamp t∗t^{*}.

proof. Consider a simplified objective where the model aims to maximize the alignment score 𝒮\mathcal{S} between a query and a ground-truth relevant event at time t∗t^{*}. The optimization follows the gradient ascent direction ∇μ𝒮\nabla_{\mu}\mathcal{S}.

The baseline attention logit is derived from the dot product of sinusoidal encodings:

𝒮base​(t∗)≈∑j=1d/2cos⁡(ωj​(t∗−μ)).\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(t^{*})\approx\sum_{j=1}^{d/2}\cos(\omega_{j}(t^{*}-\mu)). (36)

The gradient with respect to μ\mu is:

∂𝒮base∂μ=∑j=1d/2ωj​sin⁡(ωj​(t∗−μ)).\frac{\partial\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}}{\partial\mu}=\sum_{j=1}^{d/2}\omega_{j}\sin(\omega_{j}(t^{*}-\mu)). (37)

This gradient function is a superposition of high-frequency sine waves. Its sign flips repeatedly as the distance |t∗−μ||t^{*}-\mu| changes. If the initialization of μ\mu is far from t∗t^{*}, the gradient direction is determined by local periodic behavior rather than the global distance to t∗t^{*}. Consequently, the optimization is prone to getting trapped in local optima (false peaks) nearest to the initialization.

Our method incorporates an adaptive bias term ℬ⁡(t∗)=exp⁡(−(t∗−μ)22​σ2)\mathcal{B}(t^{*})=\exp\left(-\frac{(t^{*}-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right). The gradient contribution from this term is:

∂ℬ∂μ=ℬ⁡(t∗)⋅t∗−μσ2.\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}}{\partial\mu}=\mathcal{B}(t^{*})\cdot\frac{t^{*}-\mu}{\sigma^{2}}. (38)

Let Δ=t∗−μ\Delta=t^{*}-\mu be the alignment error. The sign of the gradient is determined by sgn​(Δ)\text{sgn}(\Delta):

  • •

    If μ<t∗\mu<t^{*} (Δ>0\Delta>0), the gradient is positive, pushing μ\mu towards t∗t^{*}.

  • •

    If μ>t∗\mu>t^{*} (Δ<0\Delta<0), the gradient is negative, pushing μ\mu towards t∗t^{*}.

Unlike the baseline, the term (t∗−μ)(t^{*}-\mu) acts as a linear restoring force. It provides a consistent global gradient direction that guides μ\mu towards t∗t^{*}, smoothing the optimization landscape and significantly expanding the basin of attraction for the true timestamp.

A.5 Attention Score Ratio Enhancement

Building upon the analysis in Appendix A.4, which guarantees that the learnable temporal center μ\mu converges to the ground-truth relevant timestamp t∗t^{*}, we now prove that the proposed attention mechanism effectively concentrates attention scores on these relevant nodes. Specifically, we demonstrate that our method enforces a strict probabilistic preference for events temporally close to t∗t^{*}, suppressing distant noise that the baseline model fails to filter.

Proof. Let t∗t^{*} be the ground-truth relevant timestamp. Based on the gradient guidance property proved in Appendix A.4, we assume the model has successfully learned the optimal temporal reference, i.e., μ≈t∗\mu\approx t^{*}.

Consider a relevant event erele_{\text{rel}} and an irrelevant noise event enoisee_{\text{noise}}. We define their respective temporal differences relative to the ground-truth timestamp t∗t^{*} as:

δrelevant=trelevant−t∗,\delta_{\text{relevant}}=t_{\text{relevant}}-t^{*}, (39)

and

δnoise=tnoise−t∗.\delta_{\text{noise}}=t_{\text{noise}}-t^{*}. (40)

The relevant event is temporally proximal to the target t∗t^{*}, while the noise event is distant. This structural difference is formalized by the inequality of their magnitudes:

|δrelevant|≪|δnoise|.|\delta_{\text{relevant}}|\ll|\delta_{\text{noise}}|. (41)

The baseline attention logit is 𝒮base​(δ)=∑cos⁡(ωj​δ)\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(\delta)=\sum\cos(\omega_{j}\delta). According to Bohr’s theorem on almost periodic functions (Bohr, 2018), 𝒮base\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}} does not vanish at infinity. Specifically:

lim sup|δ|→∞𝒮base​(δ)=supδ∈ℝ𝒮base​(δ).\limsup_{|\delta|\to\infty}\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(\delta)=\sup_{\delta\in\mathbb{R}}\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(\delta). (42)

This implies that there exist infinitely many distant timestamps tn​o​i​s​et_{noise} (where |δn​o​i​s​e|→∞|\delta_{noise}|\to\infty) such that:

𝒮base​(tn​o​i​s​e)≈𝒮base​(tr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t).\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(t_{noise})\approx\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(t_{relevant}). (43)

Consequently, the baseline model cannot structurally guarantee that a relevant node receives a higher score than a distant noise node. The discriminative margin Δbase=𝒮base​(tr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t)−𝒮base​(tn​o​i​s​e)\Delta_{\text{base}}=\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(t_{relevant})-\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(t_{noise}) has a lower bound of approximately 00 (or even negative values due to oscillations), indicating a failure to distinguish relevance from periodic noise.

In our method, with μ≈t∗\mu\approx t^{*}, the Gaussian bias becomes ℬ(δ)=exp(−δ2/2σ2)\mathcal{B}(\delta)=\exp(-\delta^{2}/2\sigma^{2}). The total logit is 𝒮ours​(δ)=𝒮base​(δ)+ℬ⁡(δ)\mathcal{S}_{\text{ours}}(\delta)=\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}(\delta)+\mathcal{B}(\delta).

The discriminative margin between the relevant event and the noise event is:

Δours=𝒮ours​(tr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t)−𝒮ours​(tn​o​i​s​e)=Δbase+[ℬ⁡(δr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t)−ℬ⁡(δn​o​i​s​e)].\Delta_{\text{ours}}=\mathcal{S}_{\text{ours}}(t_{relevant})-\mathcal{S}_{\text{ours}}(t_{noise})=\Delta_{\text{base}}+\left[\mathcal{B}(\delta_{relevant})-\mathcal{B}(\delta_{noise})\right]. (44)

Since |δr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t|≪|δn​o​i​s​e||\delta_{relevant}|\ll|\delta_{noise}|, and the Gaussian function is strictly monotonically decreasing with respect to distance from the center, we have:

ℬ⁡(δr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t)≫ℬ⁡(δn​o​i​s​e)≈0.\mathcal{B}(\delta_{relevant})\gg\mathcal{B}(\delta_{noise})\approx 0. (45)

Even in the worst-case scenario for the baseline (where Δbase≤0\Delta_{\text{base}}\leq 0 due to periodic misalignment), the Gaussian term introduces a strictly positive margin enhancement.

Specifically, considering the asymptotic limit where the noise becomes infinitely distant (|δn​o​i​s​e|→∞|\delta_{noise}|\to\infty) and the relevant event is perfectly aligned with the learned center (δr​e​l→0\delta_{rel}\to 0), we have:

lim|δn​o​i​s​e|→∞ℬ⁡(δn​o​i​s​e)=0andlimδr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t→0ℬ⁡(δr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t)=1.\lim_{|\delta_{noise}|\to\infty}\mathcal{B}(\delta_{noise})=0\quad\text{and}\quad\lim_{\delta_{relevant}\to 0}\mathcal{B}(\delta_{relevant})=1. (46)

This imposes a strict exponential penalty on the noise in the score ratio:

αn​o​i​s​ew/ Gαr​e​l​e​v​a​n​tw/ G=exp⁡(𝒮base​(n​o​i​s​e)−𝒮base​(r​e​l​e​v​a​n​t)−1)=e−1⋅αn​o​i​s​ew/o Gαr​e​l​e​v​a​n​tw/o G.\frac{\alpha_{noise}^{\text{w/ \ G}}}{\alpha_{relevant}^{\text{w/ \ G}}}=\exp\left(\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}({noise})-\mathcal{S}_{\text{base}}({relevant})-1\right)=e^{-1}\cdot\frac{\alpha_{noise}^{\text{w/o \ G}}}{\alpha_{relevant}^{\text{w/o \ G}}}. (47)

where αn​o​i​s​e\alpha_{noise} and αr​e​l​e​v​a​n​t\alpha_{relevant} denote the attention scores for temporal noise and related nodes, respectively; 𝐞\mathrm{\mathbf{e}} is Euler’s number; and w/ G” and w/o G” distinguish the attention mechanisms with and without Gaussian bias.

Combining the result that μ\mu converges to t∗t^{*} (Appendix A.4) with the Gaussian decay property, we prove that our method effectively assigns significantly higher attention scores to strictly temporally relevant nodes. Unlike the baseline, which is susceptible to distant "periodic ghosts," our mechanism imposes a structural envelope that filters out irrelevant temporal information, ensuring that the model’s focus remains robustly on the learned temporal context.

Appendix B Experimental Details.

B.1 Training Setting

GelGT is trained in an end-to-end manner without any pre-training stage to ensure a fair comparison with baseline methods such as RelGT. We do not adopt pre-training in our setting for two reasons: (i) it introduces significant computational overhead, and (ii) it often fails to transfer effectively across relational graphs (e.g., Griffin still underperforms even after fine-tuning). In contrast, direct supervised training allows the model to better adapt to the target relational structure, leading to more stable and competitive performance.

B.2 Benchmark Details.

In this section, we present a comprehensive overview of the datasets and evaluation tasks sourced from RelBench (Robinson et al., 2024). RelBench encompasses seven datasets spanning diverse relational database domains, such as e-commerce, clinical records, social networks, and sports. These datasets are meticulously curated from their respective domains, with training set sizes ranging from 1.3K to 5.4M records, totaling 47M training instances. Each dataset supports various predictive tasks, including modeling user engagement with advertisements within a four-day window or forecasting the primary outcomes of clinical trials over a year.

Collectively, RelBench defines 30 tasks categorized into entity classification, entity regression, and recommendation. Our evaluation focuses on 21 classification and regression tasks, as GelGT is primarily designed as a node representation learning framework for Relational Deep Learning (RDL). Following pror work (Dwivedi et al., 2026), we exclude recommendation tasks in this study due to their specific requirements, such as target node identification (You et al., 2021) or the adoption of pair-wise learning architectures (Yuan et al., 2025). Detailed statistics for all evaluated datasets and tasks are summarized in Table 11.

B.3 Datasets

In this section, we include the details on the datasets in RelBench (Robinson et al., 2024) which we use for our evaluation.

  • •

    rel-amazon. The Amazon E-commerce dataset consists of product details, user information, and review interactions from Amazon’s platform, including metadata like pricing and categories, along with review ratings and content.

  • •

    rel-avito. Avito’s marketplace dataset contains search queries, advertisement characteristics, and contextual information from this major online trading platform that facilitates transactions across various categories including real estate and vehicles.

  • •

    rel-event. The Event Recommendation dataset from Hangtime mobile app tracks users’ social planning, capturing interactions, event details, demographic data, and social connections to reveal how relationships impact user behavior.

  • •

    rel-f1. The F1 dataset provides comprehensive Formula 1 racing information since 1950, documenting drivers, constructors, manufacturers, and circuits with detailed records of race results, standings, and specific data on various racing sessions and pit stops.

  • •

    rel-hm. H&M’s dataset contains customer-product interactions from their e-commerce platform, featuring customer demographics, product descriptions, and purchase histories.

  • •

    rel-stack. The Stack Exchange dataset documents activity from this network of Q&A websites, including user biographies, posts, comments, edits, votes, and question relationships where users earn reputation through contributions.

  • •

    rel-trial. The clinical trial dataset from the AACT initiative has study protocols and outcomes, containing trial designs, participant information, intervention details, and results metrics, serving as a key resource for medical research.

Temporal information in RelBench.

We clarify that the temporal information follows the standard RelBench (Robinson et al., 2024) setting. We address four aspects explicitly.

What temporal information means. Each RelBench prediction sample has a seed time, which indicates when the prediction is made. Historical events or interactions may also have their own timestamps. GelGT uses the temporal relation between a historical neighbor’s timestamp and the seed time.

Whether it is provided by the dataset. Yes. RelBench task tables provide Entity ID, seed time, and target label. For example, rel-event/user-repeat contains user and timestamp, rel-avito/user-clicks contains UserID and timestamp, and rel-f1/driver-dnf contains driverId and date.

Whether all nodes have timestamps. No. Only time-aware event or interaction tables have time columns, such as events.start_time, event_attendees.start_time, VisitStream.ViewDate, results.date, and studies.start_date. Static entity tables such as UserInfo may not have timestamps.

Single or multiple timestamps. For a single event or interaction record, the temporal information is usually one timestamp. An entity can be connected to multiple historical records, so it may be associated with multiple timestamps through its interactions.

How GelGT uses it. The seed time filters future records and prevents temporal leakage. For the retained historical neighbors, GelGT computes their time interval to the seed time. The Gaussian temporal bias then uses this interval to model whether a historical neighbor is temporally relevant to the current prediction.

B.5 Hyperparameter Settings

Sampling Module.

In our experimental setup, to accommodate the varying demands for neighborhood information density across different downstream tasks, we employ a two-stage neighborhood sampling strategy.

We implement differentiated configurations for sampling sizes based on task characteristics. For the node classification task, we initially sample 300300 candidate neighbors in the first stage, followed by a filtering mechanism that retains 200200 nodes as input. Conversely, for the node regression task—to address potentially more complex feature dependencies—we increase the initial sampling budget to 500500 nodes, ultimately selecting 300300 nodes for model training. This tailored configuration aims to strike an optimal balance between computational efficiency and model performance.

Model Module.

Our proposed model adopts a unified hybrid architecture designed to capture both local structural topology and global temporal-semantic dependencies.

To effectively handle the heterogeneous and temporal nature of the relational graph, we employ a set of domain-specific encoders (Dwivedi et al., 2026) to project diverse input features into a unified latent space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Specifically, we utilize learnable embedding layers to encode node type heterogeneity and relative hop distances from the central node. Furthermore, continuous timestamps are processed via a TimeEncoder to preserve temporal dynamics, while raw tabular node features are encoded using a TabularEncoder based on feature statistics. To enhance subgraph structural awareness, a learnable positional encoding is also incorporated. All resulting embeddings are normalized via LayerNorm, concatenated, and projected to a dimension of d=512d=512 through a 2-layer MLP mixture network.

The core processing layer, GelGTLayer, processes the refined subgraph sequence Xi​nX_{in} through two parallel branches to extract complementary features. The GNN Branch is designed to explicitly capture local neighborhood topology using a 3-layer GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017) backbone. Each layer applies message passing followed by LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016), GELU (Hendrycks, 2016) activation, and Dropout (p=0.1p=0.1). Crucially, residual connections (He et al., 2016) are incorporated at each layer to facilitate gradient flow and prevent over-smoothing (Chen et al., 2020; Chamberlain et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018), yielding a structure-aware representation Hg​n​nH_{gnn}.

Parallel to the GNN, the Attention Branch employs a Transformer-based LocalModule to capture long-range dependencies and temporal interactions. By utilizing Multi-Head Self-Attention (Heads=44) integrated with temporal embeddings, this branch allows the model to dynamically weigh neighbors based on both semantic similarity and temporal proximity, producing a context-aware representation Ha​t​t​nH_{attn}.

To optimally combine the structural and semantic representations, we introduce a learnable gating parameter η\eta. The final representation Hf​i​n​a​lH_{final} is computed as a dynamic weighted sum:

Hf​i​n​a​l=η⋅Ha​t​t​n+(1−η)⋅Hg​n​nH_{final}=\eta\cdot H_{attn}+(1-\eta)\cdot H_{gnn} (48)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) denotes the Sigmoid function. This mechanism allows the model to adaptively balance the contribution of GNN and Transformer modules based on the specific requirements of the downstream task. Finally, a 2-layer MLP head generates the prediction.

The detailed hyperparameter configurations and implementation specifications are summarized in Table 12.
